title: Brass vs alloy vs copper base metals in jewellery
description: Brass, copper or alloy: what is under the plating of your fashion jewellery? Compare durability, weight, skin feel and repair, and know which to buy.
intro: Under the gold or silver colour, almost all fashion jewellery is built on one of three bases: brass, copper or a mixed 'alloy'. Brass is usually the best all-rounder for plated jewellery because it is strong, holds fine detail and takes plating well. Copper is soft and traditional but reacts quickly with moisture. Alloy is the cheapest and lightest, but quality varies widely. The base metal decides how long a piece lasts, how it feels on skin and whether it can be repaired, so it is worth checking before you buy.

sections.heading: Brass: the workhorse of fashion jewellery
paragraphs: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, with a natural yellow colour. That colour is useful: if the gold plating wears a little on an edge, the brass underneath is close enough in tone that it does not jump out immediately.

It is firm enough to hold stones in claws and cups, it can be cast or pressed into detailed shapes, and it bonds well with electroplating. It can also be soldered, which means a broken joint or hook can often be repaired, and a faded piece can be re-plated.

The downside is that brass darkens when exposed to moisture and air, and can leave a greenish mark on some people's skin with sweat. Good plating and a protective coat slow this down. Varaha's [Kundan necklace sets](/women/necklaces) are made on a brass base, which is common for quality Kundan work.

sections.heading: Copper: soft, warm and reactive
paragraphs: Copper is a pure metal with a reddish-pink colour. It is soft and easy to shape, so it is used for hand-hammered bangles, rustic pieces and some traditional designs, sometimes left unplated for its natural colour.

Copper reacts with sweat and humidity faster than brass. This is why unplated copper often leaves a green tint on the wrist or neck, and why plated copper can develop dark or green spots where the plating thins. The mark on skin washes off, but it can be annoying on a white kurta collar.
Some people wear copper bracelets for traditional reasons. That is a personal choice; for jewellery durability, copper simply needs more care to keep its look.

sections.heading: Alloy: the widest category
paragraphs: 'Alloy' on a listing usually means a mix of metals, often zinc-based, sometimes with others added. It can be cast into intricate shapes cheaply, which is why it appears in many budget earrings, oxidised pieces and lightweight chokers.

Because the word can describe so many recipes, quality varies more than with brass. A well-made alloy piece can look great and feel pleasantly light. A poor one can be brittle, snapping rather than bending when dropped, and difficult to repair because many alloys do not solder easily. Some alloys may also contain nickel, which matters if you have sensitive skin.

sections.heading: Quick comparison
paragraphs: Use this as a simple reference when you read product descriptions:
list: Strength: brass is strong and holds stones well; copper is soft and bends easily; alloy depends on the mix and can be brittle.
Weight: brass and copper feel solid; alloy is usually lighter.
Detail: brass and alloy both take fine detail; copper suits simpler or hammered designs.
Plating: brass takes plating very well; copper plates well but reacts if exposed; alloy needs good surface preparation.
Repair and re-plating: brass is usually the easiest; copper is possible; many alloys are difficult.
Price: alloy is generally cheapest, brass in the middle.

sections.heading: How to guess the base metal yourself
paragraphs: If a listing does not say, a few clues help. Look at worn areas or the inside of a hook: a yellow tone suggests brass, a pinkish-red tone suggests copper, and a grey or dull white tone suggests an alloy. Weight is another hint, since alloy pieces of the same size usually feel noticeably lighter.
A magnet will not help much, since brass, copper and most jewellery alloys are not magnetic. The simplest and most reliable method is still to ask the seller directly.

sections.heading: Which one should you choose?
paragraphs: For bridal and festive sets you will wear repeatedly, brass is usually worth the slightly higher price because of its strength, detail and repair options. For quirky, light everyday earrings that you may not wear for years, a good alloy is perfectly sensible. Choose copper when you love its natural colour and are happy to give it a quick wipe after each wear.

Whatever the base, care follows the same rules: keep it dry, keep perfume off it, and store it in a closed pouch. If silver tone is what you want and you would rather avoid plated base metals altogether, solid [925 sterling silver](/silver) is the next step up.

faq.a: Brass is one of the better bases for plated fashion jewellery. It is strong, holds detail and takes plating well, though it still needs to be kept dry.

faq.q: What does alloy mean in jewellery?
faq.a: It means a mix of metals, often zinc-based. It is light and inexpensive, but quality and durability vary a lot.

faq.q: Why does copper jewellery turn my skin green?
faq.a: Copper reacts with sweat and moisture, forming a green layer that can transfer to skin. It washes off and is common with unplated copper.

faq.q: Which base metal is best for sensitive skin?
faq.a: None of these is ideal for very sensitive skin. Look for nickel-free labelling or consider 925 sterling silver instead.
